strengths: Addresses important practical problem: significant efficiency gap between single-vector and multi-vector retrieval systems limits adoption of superior multi-vector models
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 7 different embedding models (5 text + 2 visual) and 6 BEIR datasets demonstrates robustness and practical value
Consistent substantial speedups (5-11x at 80% recall on ColBERTv2, even larger on other models) with particularly strong results on non-ColBERTv2 embeddings where baselines struggle
Sound technical approach: clever exploitation of MaxSim decomposability and linear output layer to enable reduction to single-vector ANNS in learned latent space
Thorough ablation studies (latent dimension, ANNS vs exact inference, training set selection) with detailed analysis in appendices
Well-written, clearly presented paper with helpful visualizations and honest discussion of limitations
Practical implementation details and scalable training strategy enable reproducibility and adoption
Robustness across different training set selections suggests good generalization and practical flexibility
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core contribution is incremental—a learned version of MUVERA's reduction approach using supervised learning instead of fixed encodings
Missing code URL at submission time raises reproducibility concerns; while open-source release is promised, code should ideally be available during review
Lack of theoretical analysis: no explanation of why MSE loss on token-level predictions leads to good document-level ranking, or analysis of approximation error propagation
Scalability analysis gaps: OLS solution requires computation per document (Eq. 7); for billion-scale corpora, indexing cost not thoroughly analyzed
Training set selection design underexplored: default approach uses corpus+query encoder (practical but suboptimal per Appendix D.2); justification for not using actual queries by default is unclear

Comparison with MUVERA uses different embedding dimensions (d'=2048 vs 10,240); while Figure 2 addresses this, equal-dimension comparisons would isolate learned vs fixed encoding benefits more clearly
Limited experimental scope: all experiments on 40 CPU cores (Intel Xeon Gold 6230); no GPU results despite GPUs being standard for dense retrieval with potentially different latency profiles
Reranking cost at high recall (>95%) is significant but deserves deeper analysis of k' vs latency tradeoff
No confidence intervals, error bars, or variance analysis despite likely multiple experimental runs
Missing analysis of failure cases or embedding model characteristics that affect performance

strengths: Sound technical approach with correct mathematical formulation and elegant decomposition of MaxSim approximation as supervised learning problem
Comprehensive evaluation across 7 datasets (6 BEIR + ViDoRe) and 7 embedding models (5 text + 2 visual), going beyond standard ColBERTv2 benchmarking
Strong empirical results: 5-11x speedup over baselines at 80% recall, with particularly notable improvements on modern embedding models where competitors fail

Important contribution to benchmarking practices: demonstrates that MUVERA fails on answerai-colbert, GTE-ModernColBERT, and LFM2-ColBERT, highlighting value of learned vs. data-oblivious representations
Practical utility: simple two-layer MLP, fast indexing (1000+ docs/sec), easy integration with existing ANNS libraries, consistent hyperparameters across experiments
Thorough ablation studies on latent dimension and ANNS vs. exact inference, with additional robustness analysis across multiple training set selection strategies (Appendix D)
Clear, well-structured presentation with effective figures and comprehensive appendices supporting reproducibility; promised open-source release
weaknesses: Theoretical justification for training set selection is limited: using corpus documents encoded with query encoder creates distribution mismatch with actual queries; while Appendix D shows empirical robustness, underlying reasons for why this works remain unexplained

Loss function choice (MSE) not justified relative to alternatives: no comparison to ranking-specific losses (triplet, contrastive, listwise) that might better align with downstream top-k retrieval objective

Limited conceptual novelty: individual components (MLP for multi-output regression, ANNS libraries for inner product search) are standard; novelty primarily lies in the application combination rather than fundamentally new techniques
Incomplete analysis of scalable training approach in Section 4.3: limited justification for why feature encoder trained on subset m' generalizes to all m documents, no ablation on subset size
Visual document results show weaker improvements (Figure 6) with notably narrower performance gaps compared to text models; limited discussion of whether this represents fundamental limitation
Missing failure mode and edge case analysis: no discussion of when method underperforms, behavior with very small/large k, or analysis of approximation error distribution across queries/documents

Some design choices lack thorough justification: network depth fixed at 2 layers without extensive alternatives testing, pooling strategy (simple sum) not compared to alternatives (mean, attention-based), activation function choices not ablated
Code repository URL is incomplete in submission ('available at' with no actual link provided)

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real latency bottleneck in multi-vector retrieval with clear practical impact (5-16x speedups)
Clean mathematical formulation decomposing MaxSim approximation as supervised learning on support functions with elegant reduction to single-vector search
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8 BEIR + visual datasets with 5 text and 2 visual embedding models, showing consistent improvements over 4 baselines
Thorough robustness analysis demonstrating method works across different training sets, even with random hidden layer weights (ELM variant)
Excellent reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, fair comparisons using identical ANNS libraries, and extensive supplementary results
Practical implementation quality: simple 2-layer MLP enabling fast training (~4.8 hours for 8.8M documents), CPU/GPU compatible, scales linearly
Strong performance across diverse models, particularly outperforming baselines on non-ColBERTv2 embeddings where competitors struggle significantly
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is applying standard MLP regression to approximate MaxSim with insight primarily in application rather than methodology
Corpus-specific training requirement limits applicability in dynamic systems; acknowledged as operational challenge for incremental indexing as documents arrive

Weak theoretical analysis: universal approximation theorem is standard and provides no insight into sample complexity or convergence rates; no formal connection between point-wise approximation error and ranking accuracy
Training set selection (corpus documents with query encoder) is somewhat ad-hoc; explanation for robustness via 'common semantic space' lacks rigorous justification

Incomplete characterization of failure modes and method limitations: why performance gap is smaller on visual retrieval (Figure 5) receives only vague explanation; no systematic analysis of when LEMUR underperforms
Memory and storage analysis under-explored: weight vector storage in ANNS index not quantified, comparison of total system memory across methods missing, quantization mentioned but not evaluated
Cost breakdown between ANNS search and MaxSim reranking not detailed; sensitivity to k' (candidate set size) not thoroughly analyzed

Comparison with MUVERA lacks depth: while supervision advantage is clear, unclear why learned representations achieve such dramatic efficiency improvements at lower dimensionality compared to data-oblivious FDEs
